claim: C. elegans avoids Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA14) in part by detecting PA14-produced NO.
source: We show that C. elegans avoids Pseudomonas aeruginosa (PA14) in part by detecting PA14-produced NO.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that PA14 mutants deficient for NO production fail to elicit avoidance and NO donors repel worms.

claim: PA14 mutants deficient for NO production fail to elicit avoidance.
source: PA14 mutants deficient for NO production fail to elicit avoidance and NO donors repel worms.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing behavioral responses to PA14 mutants.

claim: NO donors repel worms.
source: PA14 mutants deficient for NO production fail to elicit avoidance and NO donors repel worms.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing behavioral avoidance responses to NO donors.

claim: PA14 and NO avoidance are mediated by a chemosensory neuron (ASJ).
source: PA14 and NO avoidance are mediated by a chemosensory neuron (ASJ) and these responses require receptor guanylate cyclases and cyclic nucleotide gated ion channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that ASJ-specific rescue and ablation experiments affect avoidance behavior.

claim: PA14 and NO avoidance responses require receptor guanylate cyclases.
source: PA14 and NO avoidance are mediated by a chemosensory neuron (ASJ) and these responses require receptor guanylate cyclases and cyclic nucleotide gated ion channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that mutations in receptor guanylate cyclases affect avoidance behavior.

claim: PA14 and NO avoidance responses require cyclic nucleotide gated ion channels.
source: PA14 and NO avoidance are mediated by a chemosensory neuron (ASJ) and these responses require receptor guanylate cyclases and cyclic nucleotide gated ion channels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that mutations in cyclic nucleotide gated ion channels affect avoidance behavior.

claim: ASJ exhibits calcium increases at both the onset and removal of NO.
source: ASJ exhibits calcium increases at both the onset and removal of NO.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: NO-evoked ON and OFF calcium transients are affected by a redox sensing protein, TRX-1/thioredoxin.
source: These NO-evoked ON and OFF calcium transients are affected by a redox sensing protein, TRX-1/thioredoxin.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing altered calcium responses in TRX-1 mutants.

claim: TRX-1's trans-nitrosylation activity inhibits the ON transient.
source: TRX-1's trans-nitrosylation activity inhibits the ON transient whereas TRX-1's de-nitrosylation activity promotes the OFF transient.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from TRX-1 mutants with specific cysteine mutations affecting trans-nitrosylation activity.

claim: TRX-1's de-nitrosylation activity promotes the OFF transient.
source: TRX-1's trans-nitrosylation activity inhibits the ON transient whereas TRX-1's de-nitrosylation activity promotes the OFF transient.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from TRX-1 mutants with specific cysteine mutations affecting de-nitrosylation activity.

claim: C. elegans exploits bacterially produced NO as a cue to mediate avoidance.
source: Thus, C. elegans exploits bacterially produced NO as a cue to mediate avoidance and TRX-1 endows ASJ with a bi-phasic response to NO exposure.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing avoidance behavior in response to PA14-produced NO and NO donors.

claim: TRX-1 endows ASJ with a bi-phasic response to NO exposure.
source: Thus, C. elegans exploits bacterially produced NO as a cue to mediate avoidance and TRX-1 endows ASJ with a bi-phasic response to NO exposure.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that TRX-1 affects both ON and OFF calcium transients in ASJ.

claim: NO regulates key physiological events in mammals, such as vasodilation, inflammatory response, and neurotransmission.
source: In mammals, NO regulates key physiological events, such as vasodilation, inflammatory response, and neurotransmission (Feelisch and Martin, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: NO regulates innate immunity and life span in the nematode C. elegans.
source: NO regulates innate immunity and life span in the nematode C. elegans (Gusarov et al., 2013), as well as virulence and biofilm formation in different bacteria (Cutruzzolà and Frankenberg-Dinkel, 2016; Shatalin et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: NO regulates virulence and biofilm formation in different bacteria.
source: NO regulates innate immunity and life span in the nematode C. elegans (Gusarov et al., 2013), as well as virulence and biofilm formation in different bacteria (Cutruzzolà and Frankenberg-Dinkel, 2016; Shatalin et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NO covalently modifies the thiol side chain of reactive cysteine residues (forming S-nitrosylated adducts), thereby modulating the activity of these proteins.
source: As a reactive oxygen species, NO covalently modifies the thiol side chain of reactive cysteine residues (forming S-nitrosylated adducts), thereby modulating the activity of these proteins (Foster et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: NO can bind to the heme co-factor associated with soluble guanylate cyclases (sGCs), thereby stimulating cGMP production and activating downstream cGMP targets.
source: NO can also bind to the heme co-factor associated with soluble guanylate cyclases (sGCs), thereby stimulating cGMP production and activating downstream cGMP targets (Denninger and Marletta, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Almost all living organisms, including bacteria, fungi, plants and animals, are able to produce NO with nitric oxide synthases (NOS).
source: Almost all living organisms, including bacteria, fungi, plants and animals, are able to produce NO with nitric oxide synthases (NOS) (Ghosh and Salerno, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: NO readily diffuses throughout the surrounding tissues to regulate cellular physiology due to its small molecular weight and gaseous nature.
source: Due to its small molecular weight and gaseous nature, NO readily diffuses throughout the surrounding tissues to regulate cellular physiology.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about the physical properties of NO.

claim: NO is released into air, where it may function as an environmental cue.
source: NO is also released into air, where it may function as an environmental cue.
evidence: This claim involves speculation about the potential function of NO in the environment.

claim: Lightning generates the major abiotic source of environmental NO.
source: Lightning generates the major abiotic source of environmental NO (Navarro-González et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: It remains unclear if NO is utilized as a sensory cue by terrestrial animals to elicit behavioral responses.
source: Despite its prevalence in the environment, it remains unclear if NO is utilized as a sensory cue by terrestrial animals to elicit behavioral responses.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in current scientific knowledge.

claim: sGCs are the only described sensors for biosynthetically produced NO, mediating NO-evoked muscle relaxation and vasodilation.
source: sGCs are the only described sensors for biosynthetically produced NO, mediating NO-evoked muscle relaxation and vasodilation (Gow et al., 2002; Stoll et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It is unclear if sGCs also play a role in NO-evoked sensory responses.
source: However, it is unclear if sGCs also play a role in NO-evoked sensory responses.
evidence: This claim identifies a gap in current scientific knowledge.

claim: In vertebrates, NO modulates the activities of various ion channels, either directly through S-nitrosylation or indirectly through sGCs.
source: In vertebrates, NO modulates the activities of various ion channels, either directly through S-nitrosylation or indirectly through sGCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NO regulation of ion channels alters neuron and muscle excitability.
source: NO regulation of ion channels alters neuron and muscle excitability (Bolotina et al., 1994; Broillet and Firestein, 1996, 1997; Koh et al., 1995; Wang et al., 2012; Wilson and Garthwaite, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In salamander olfactory sensory neurons, S-nitrosylation of a cysteine residue in cyclic nucleotide-gated (CNG) channels activates these channels, thereby directly altering odor-evoked responses in these cells.
source: For example, in salamander olfactory sensory neurons, S-nitrosylation of a cysteine residue in cyclic nucleotide-gated (CNG) channels activates these channels, thereby directly altering odor-evoked responses in these cells (Broillet and Firestein, 1996, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CNG channels are highly conserved among invertebrates and vertebrates.
source: CNG channels are highly conserved among invertebrates and vertebrates.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about CNG channel evolution.

claim: Both CNG channels and guanylate cyclases are essential for transducing responses for many sensory modalities.
source: Because both CNG channels and guanylate cyclases are essential for transducing responses for many sensory modalities, these results suggest that CNG channels and guanylate cyclases may also play a role in NO-evoked sensory responses.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about sensory transduction mechanisms.

claim: CNG channels and guanylate cyclases may play a role in NO-evoked sensory responses.
source: Because both CNG channels and guanylate cyclases are essential for transducing responses for many sensory modalities, these results suggest that CNG channels and guanylate cyclases may also play a role in NO-evoked sensory responses.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the known roles of CNG channels and guanylate cyclases in sensory transduction.

claim: The nematode C. elegans lacks genes encoding NOS.
source: Unlike most metazoans, the nematode C. elegans lacks genes encoding NOS (Gusarov et al., 2013) and consequently cannot synthesize NO.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: C. elegans cannot synthesize NO.
source: Unlike most metazoans, the nematode C. elegans lacks genes encoding NOS (Gusarov et al., 2013) and consequently cannot synthesize NO.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the lack of NOS genes in C. elegans.

claim: C. elegans is exposed to several potential environmental sources of NO, including NO produced by bacteria, which regulates C. elegans stress responses and aging.
source: Nonetheless, C. elegans is exposed to several potential environmental sources of NO, including NO produced by bacteria, which regulates C. elegans stress responses and aging (Gusarov et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: C. elegans lives in rotting organic matter, where it feeds on diverse microbes, including the gram-negative bacteria from the Pseudomonas and the Bacillus genera.
source: C. elegans lives in rotting organic matter, where it feeds on diverse microbes, including the gram-negative bacteria from the Pseudomonas and the Bacillus genera (Samuel et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: C. elegans exhibits a rich repertoire of behavioral interactions with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Serratia marascens, and Bacillus subtilis.
source: C. elegans exhibits a rich repertoire of behavioral interactions with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Serratia marascens, and Bacillus subtilis (Brandt and Ringstad, 2015; Garsin et al., 2003; Reddy et al., 2009; Styer et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A few bacterially derived metabolites have been shown to mediate behavioral responses in C. elegans.
source: A few bacterially derived metabolites have been shown to mediate these behavioral responses (Brandt and Ringstad, 2015; Meisel and Kim, 2014; Pradel et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: When cultured with a non-pathogenic Escherichia coli strain as the food source, C elegans spends most of its time foraging inside the bacterial lawn.
source: When cultured with a non-pathogenic Escherichia coli strain as the food source, C elegans spends most of its time foraging inside the bacterial lawn (Bendesky et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: When feeding on a pathogenic bacterial strain (e.g. P. aeruginosa PA14), C. elegans avoids the pathogen by foraging off the bacterial lawn.
source: By contrast, when feeding on a pathogenic bacterial strain (e.g. P. aeruginosa PA14), C. elegans avoids the pathogen by foraging off the bacterial lawn (Reddy et al., 2009; Styer et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Over a time course of a few hours the majority of the wild-type adult animals remained off the PA14 lawn.
source: Consistent with prior findings, over a time course of a few hours the majority of the wild-type adult animals remained off the PA14 lawn (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: PA14 avoidance is contingent on the virulence of the bacterial strain.
source: PA14 avoidance is contingent on the virulence of the bacterial strain, as an isogenic PA14 gacA mutant, which is significantly impaired in its ability to kill C. elegans (Tan et al., 1999), failed to elicit avoidance of the bacterial lawn (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and a citation to prior literature.

claim: An isogenic PA14 gacA mutant is significantly impaired in its ability to kill C. elegans.
source: PA14 avoidance is contingent on the virulence of the bacterial strain, as an isogenic PA14 gacA mutant, which is significantly impaired in its ability to kill C. elegans (Tan et al., 1999), failed to elicit avoidance of the bacterial lawn (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: An isogenic PA14 gacA mutant failed to elicit avoidance of the bacterial lawn.
source: PA14 avoidance is contingent on the virulence of the bacterial strain, as an isogenic PA14 gacA mutant, which is significantly impaired in its ability to kill C. elegans (Tan et al., 1999), failed to elicit avoidance of the bacterial lawn (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: P. aeruginosa produces NO via a biosynthetic pathway that converts nitrite to NO with nitrite reductase (nir).
source: P. aeruginosa produces NO via a biosynthetic pathway that converts nitrite to NO with nitrite reductase (nir) (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by a diagram shown in Figure 2A and is based on established knowledge of bacterial NO biosynthesis.

claim: A PA14 mutant carrying a nirS mutation exhibits decreased ability to kill infected C. elegans, likely due to the decreased expression of virulence factors.
source: Prior studies reported that a PA14 mutant carrying a nirS mutation exhibits decreased ability to kill infected C. elegans, likely due to the decreased expression of virulence factors (Van Alst et al., 2007, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Avoidance of nirS mutants was dramatically reduced compared to wild-type PA14 controls.
source: We found that avoidance of nirS mutants was dramatically reduced compared to wild-type PA14 controls (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When placed inside a non-pathogenic E. coli (OP50 strain) lawn, two different NO donors (MAHMA NONOate and DPTA NONOate) elicited C. elegans avoidance.
source: When placed inside a non-pathogenic E. coli (OP50 strain) lawn, two different NO donors (MAHMA NONOate and DPTA NONOate) elicited C. elegans avoidance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: After a 30 min exposure, the majority of animals remained out of the NO-tainted E. coli lawn, similarly to the avoidance elicited by the PA14 lawn.
source: After a 30 min exposure, the majority of animals remained out of the NO-tainted E. coli lawn, similarly to the avoidance elicited by the PA14 lawn (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Bacterially produced NO is required for PA14 avoidance.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that bacterially produced NO is required for PA14 avoidance and suggests that C. elegans responds to NO as a repulsive chemosensory cue.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that nirS mutants fail to elicit avoidance and NO donors elicit avoidance.

claim: C. elegans responds to NO as a repulsive chemosensory cue.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that bacterially produced NO is required for PA14 avoidance and suggests that C. elegans responds to NO as a repulsive chemosensory cue.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing avoidance behavior in response to NO.

claim: CNG channels mediate many C. elegans chemosensory responses.
source: CNG channels mediate many C. elegans chemosensory responses.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about CNG channels in C. elegans.

claim: TAX-4/CNGα and TAX-2/CNGβ form a heteromeric cGMP-gated cation channel.
source: The C. elegans genome contains several genes that encode CNG channel subunits, including TAX-4/CNGα and TAX-2/CNGβ, which form a heteromeric cGMP-gated cation channel (Komatsu et al., 1999) and are expressed in several classes of chemosensory neurons (Coburn et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TAX-4/CNGα and TAX-2/CNGβ are expressed in several classes of chemosensory neurons.
source: The C. elegans genome contains several genes that encode CNG channel subunits, including TAX-4/CNGα and TAX-2/CNGβ, which form a heteromeric cGMP-gated cation channel (Komatsu et al., 1999) and are expressed in several classes of chemosensory neurons (Coburn et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: PA14 and NO donor avoidance were abolished in tax-4(p678) mutants.
source: PA14 and NO donor avoidance were abolished in tax-4(p678) mutants (Figures 2B and 3C), which contain a putative null mutation in tax-4.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2B and 3C.

claim: tax-4(p678) mutants contain a putative null mutation in tax-4.
source: PA14 and NO donor avoidance were abolished in tax-4(p678) mutants (Figures 2B and 3C), which contain a putative null mutation in tax-4.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the tax-4(p678) allele.

claim: Similar PA14 and NO avoidance defects were observed in the tax-2(p671) mutants.
source: Similar PA14 and NO avoidance defects were also observed in the tax-2(p671) mutants (Figure 2D and E), which contain a strong loss of function mutation in tax-2.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2D and E.

claim: tax-2(p671) mutants contain a strong loss of function mutation in tax-2.
source: Similar PA14 and NO avoidance defects were also observed in the tax-2(p671) mutants (Figure 2D and E), which contain a strong loss of function mutation in tax-2.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the tax-2(p671) allele.

claim: TAX-4/CNGα and TAX-2/CNGβ subunits are both required for proper avoidance behavior.
source: Thus, TAX-4/CNGα and TAX-2/CNGβ subunits were both required for proper avoidance behavior.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that mutations in both genes abolish avoidance behavior.

claim: The cGMP-gated sensory channel TAX-4/TAX-2 is required for NO and PA14 avoidance.
source: Taken together, these results show that the cGMP-gated sensory channel TAX-4/TAX-2 is required for NO and PA14 avoidance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that mutations in TAX-4 and TAX-2 abolish avoidance behavior.

claim: TAX-4/TAX-2 channels mediate several chemosensory responses.
source: Because TAX-4/TAX-2 channels mediate several chemosensory responses, these results further support the idea that C. elegans responds to NO as a repulsive environmental odorant.
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about TAX-4/TAX-2 channels.

claim: C. elegans responds to NO as a repulsive environmental odorant.
source: Because TAX-4/TAX-2 channels mediate several chemosensory responses, these results further support the idea that C. elegans responds to NO as a repulsive environmental odorant.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the requirement for TAX-4/TAX-2 channels in NO avoidance.

claim: A transgene expressing tax-4 selectively in ASJ sensory neurons (using the trx-1 promoter) fully rescued PA14 avoidance defects exhibited by tax-4(p678) mutants.
source: By contrast, a transgene expressing tax-4 selectively in ASJ sensory neurons (using the trx-1 promoter) (Miranda-Vizuete et al., 2006) fully rescued PA14 avoidance and partially rescued NO donor avoidance defects exhibited by tax-4(p678) mutants (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A and C.

claim: A transgene expressing tax-4 selectively in ASJ sensory neurons partially rescued NO donor avoidance defects exhibited by tax-4(p678) mutants.
source: By contrast, a transgene expressing tax-4 selectively in ASJ sensory neurons (using the trx-1 promoter) (Miranda-Vizuete et al., 2006) fully rescued PA14 avoidance and partially rescued NO donor avoidance defects exhibited by tax-4(p678) mutants (Figure 3A and C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3A and C.

claim: TAX-4 CNG channels act in the ASJ neurons to promote PA14 and NO donor avoidance.
source: Thus, TAX-4 CNG channels act in the ASJ neurons to promote PA14 and NO donor avoidance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that ASJ-specific expression of tax-4 rescues avoidance defects.

claim: Inducing ASJ cell death significantly decreased PA14 and NO donor avoidance.
source: As expected, inducing ASJ cell death significantly decreased PA14 and NO donor avoidance (Figure 3E–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3E-F.

claim: ASJ neurons respond to two bacterial metabolites to mediate PA14 avoidance.
source: A prior study showed that ASJ neurons respond to two bacterial metabolites to mediate PA14 avoidance (Meisel and Kim, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: ASJ neurons sense PA14-derived NO as a repulsive cue through the TAX-2/TAX-4 CNG channels, thereby promoting avoidance of virulent PA14 strains.
source: Here, we show that ASJ neurons also sense PA14-derived NO as a repulsive cue through the TAX-2/TAX-4 CNG channels, thereby promoting avoidance of virulent PA14 strains.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that ASJ neurons are required for NO avoidance and that TAX-2/TAX-4 channels are required in ASJ.

claim: Exposure to NO donor evoked a significant increase in GCaMP6s fluorescence in the ASJ neurons, reaching peak intensity within a few seconds and gradually returning to baseline fluorescence despite the continuing exposure to NO.
source: Exposure to NO donor evoked a significant increase in GCaMP6s fluorescence in the ASJ neurons, reaching peak intensity within a few seconds and gradually returning to baseline fluorescence despite the continuing exposure to NO (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Removing the NO stimulus evoked an ASJ calcium transient that lasted ~20 s.
source: Removing the NO stimulus also evoked an ASJ calcium transient that lasted ~20 s (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Switching between streams of control buffer solution did not alter the GCaMP6s signal in ASJ.
source: By contrast, switching between streams of control buffer solution did not alter the GCaMP6s signal in ASJ (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The ON and OFF responses of ASJ to NO remained intact in unc-13 mutants.
source: We found that the ON and OFF responses of ASJ to NO remained intact in unc-13 mutants (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that NO-evoked ASJ calcium transients are unlikely to result from indirect activation of ASJ by synaptic input.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: NO-evoked ASJ calcium transients are unlikely to result from indirect activation of ASJ by synaptic input.
source: We found that the ON and OFF responses of ASJ to NO remained intact in unc-13 mutants (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), suggesting that NO-evoked ASJ calcium transients are unlikely to result from indirect activation of ASJ by synaptic input.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that blocking synaptic transmission does not affect ASJ responses to NO.

claim: The ASJ sensory neurons directly sense NO.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that the ASJ sensory neurons directly sense NO, and that ASJ neurons have a biphasic response to NO, exhibiting increased cytoplasmic calcium at both NO onset and removal (hereafter indicated as ON and OFF responses).
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that ASJ responds to NO even when synaptic transmission is blocked.

claim: ASJ neurons have a biphasic response to NO, exhibiting increased cytoplasmic calcium at both NO onset and removal.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that the ASJ sensory neurons directly sense NO, and that ASJ neurons have a biphasic response to NO, exhibiting increased cytoplasmic calcium at both NO onset and removal (hereafter indicated as ON and OFF responses).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data showing ON and OFF responses.

claim: The tax-4(p678) mutation abolished the ASJ response to the onset and the removal of NO.
source: The tax-4(p678) mutation, which abolished PA14 and NO donor avoidance (Figures 2B and 3A–C), also eliminated the NO-evoked ON and OFF calcium transients in ASJ (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: A transgene selectively restoring tax-4 expression in ASJ reinstated the NO-evoked ON calcium transients in ASJ.
source: A transgene selectively restoring tax-4 expression in ASJ reinstated the NO-evoked ON calcium transients in ASJ (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Activation of TAX-4 channels in the ASJ sensory neurons generates increased calcium transients in response to NO exposure, which results in NO avoidance behavior.
source: These results indicate that activation of TAX-4 channels in the ASJ sensory neurons generates increased calcium transients in response to NO exposure, which results in NO avoidance behavior.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that TAX-4 is required for both calcium responses and avoidance behavior.

claim: The requirement for TAX-2/TAX-4 CNG channels for NO sensation suggests that NO stimulates cGMP synthesis in ASJ.
source: The requirement for TAX-2/TAX-4 CNG channels for NO sensation suggests that NO stimulates cGMP synthesis in ASJ.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the known function of TAX-2/TAX-4 as cGMP-gated channels.

claim: Responses to extracellular gaseous ligands, such as O2 and NO, are often mediated by sGCs.
source: Responses to extracellular gaseous ligands, such as O2 and NO, are often mediated by sGCs; however, none of the sGC encoding genes is expressed in ASJ neurons (www.wormbase.org).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about sGCs.

claim: None of the sGC encoding genes is expressed in ASJ neurons.
source: Responses to extracellular gaseous ligands, such as O2 and NO, are often mediated by sGCs; however, none of the sGC encoding genes is expressed in ASJ neurons (www.wormbase.org).
evidence: This claim is based on gene expression data from WormBase.

claim: Receptor guanylate cyclases (rGCs) mediate C. elegans responses to CO2.
source: Receptor guanylate cyclases (rGCs) mediate C. elegans responses to CO2 (Hallem et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: ASJ neurons express two rGCs (GCY-27 and DAF-11).
source: ASJ neurons express two rGCs (GCY-27 and DAF-11) (www.wormbase.org).
evidence: This claim is based on gene expression data from WormBase.

claim: PA14 and NO donor avoidance were both abolished in daf-11(m47) mutants.
source: We found that PA14 and NO donor avoidance were both abolished in daf-11(m47) mutants (which contain a temperature sensitive loss of function mutation) and both avoidance responses were reinstated by a transgene that expresses daf-11 in the ASJ neurons (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: daf-11(m47) mutants contain a temperature sensitive loss of function mutation.
source: We found that PA14 and NO donor avoidance were both abolished in daf-11(m47) mutants (which contain a temperature sensitive loss of function mutation) and both avoidance responses were reinstated by a transgene that expresses daf-11 in the ASJ neurons (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the daf-11(m47) allele.

claim: Both PA14 and NO donor avoidance responses were reinstated by a transgene that expresses daf-11 in the ASJ neurons.
source: We found that PA14 and NO donor avoidance were both abolished in daf-11(m47) mutants (which contain a temperature sensitive loss of function mutation) and both avoidance responses were reinstated by a transgene that expresses daf-11 in the ASJ neurons (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The daf-11(m47) mutation completely abolished the ASJ ON and OFF response to NO donor.
source: We found that the daf-11(m47) mutation completely abolished the ASJ ON and OFF response to NO donor (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expressing the daf-11 cDNA specifically in ASJ partially rescued the ASJ ON response to NO donor.
source: Expressing the daf-11 cDNA specifically in ASJ partially rescued the ASJ ON response to NO donor (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutations inactivating GCY-27 decreased but did not abolish PA14 avoidance.
source: In contrast to DAF-11, mutations inactivating GCY-27 decreased but did not abolish PA14 avoidance and had no effect on the ASJ ON response, although they did eliminate the ASJ OFF response to NO donor (Figure 5B and E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutations inactivating GCY-27 had no effect on the ASJ ON response.
source: In contrast to DAF-11, mutations inactivating GCY-27 decreased but did not abolish PA14 avoidance and had no effect on the ASJ ON response, although they did eliminate the ASJ OFF response to NO donor (Figure 5B and E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutations inactivating GCY-27 eliminated the ASJ OFF response to NO donor.
source: In contrast to DAF-11, mutations inactivating GCY-27 decreased but did not abolish PA14 avoidance and had no effect on the ASJ ON response, although they did eliminate the ASJ OFF response to NO donor (Figure 5B and E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rGCs DAF-11 and GCY-27 function in the ASJ neurons to mediate NO sensation.
source: Together, these results indicate that the rGCs DAF-11 and GCY-27 function in the ASJ neurons to mediate NO sensation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that mutations in these genes affect NO responses in ASJ.

claim: The predicted DAF-11 protein does not contain a heme-NO-binding (HNOB) domain.
source: The predicted DAF-11 protein does not contain a heme-NO-binding (HNOB) domain, although it contains a heme-NO-binding associated (HNOBA) domain (www.wormbase.org).
evidence: This claim is based on protein domain predictions from WormBase.

claim: The predicted DAF-11 protein contains a heme-NO-binding associated (HNOBA) domain.
source: The predicted DAF-11 protein does not contain a heme-NO-binding (HNOB) domain, although it contains a heme-NO-binding associated (HNOBA) domain (www.wormbase.org).
evidence: This claim is based on protein domain predictions from WormBase.

claim: HNOB domains are found in proteins that directly bind heme cofactors.
source: HNOB domains are found in proteins that directly bind heme cofactors whereas HNOBA domains are similar to PAS domains and are found in a subset of HNOB containing proteins (Iyer et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: HNOBA domains are similar to PAS domains and are found in a subset of HNOB containing proteins.
source: HNOB domains are found in proteins that directly bind heme cofactors whereas HNOBA domains are similar to PAS domains and are found in a subset of HNOB containing proteins (Iyer et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The daf-11(nu629) mutation abolished the ASJ response to both the onset and the removal of NO.
source: The resulting daf-11(nu629) mutation abolished the ASJ response to both the onset and the removal of NO (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that DAF-11 mediates NO sensing by interacting with other NO-binding proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: DAF-11 mediates NO sensing by interacting with other NO-binding proteins.
source: The resulting daf-11(nu629) mutation abolished the ASJ response to both the onset and the removal of NO (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1), suggesting that DAF-11 mediates NO sensing by interacting with other NO-binding proteins.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that deleting the HNOBA domain abolishes NO responses.

claim: NO acts as an external sensory cue.
source: NO is freely diffusible and membrane permeable; consequently, PA14 produced NO could act as either an external sensory cue or by directly activating intracellular signaling pathways in ASJ.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that NO sensing requires functional ciliated sensory endings.

claim: Two cilia defective mutants, osm-12(n1606) null mutants and bbs-9(gk471) null mutants, were both defective in avoiding the lawn of PA14 and the NO donor.
source: Two cilia defective mutants, osm-12(n1606) null mutants and bbs-9(gk471) null mutants, were both defective in avoiding the lawn of PA14 and the NO donor (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6A and B.

claim: The normal function of sensory cilia is required for the NO sensation.
source: These results indicate that the normal function of sensory cilia is required for the NO sensation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that cilia defective mutants are defective in NO avoidance.

claim: Avoidance of NO and the PA14 lawn were both defective in daf-25(m362) mutants.
source: Avoidance of NO and the PA14 lawn were both defective in daf-25(m362) mutants (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 6A and B.

claim: The defect in PA14 avoidance in daf-25(m362) mutants was partially rescued by a transgene that restores DAF-25 expression in ASJ neurons.
source: The defect in PA14 avoidance was partially rescued by a transgene that restores DAF-25 expression in ASJ neurons (Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The NO evoked ON and OFF calcium transients in ASJ were completely abolished in daf-25(m362) mutants.
source: As in daf-11(m47) mutants, the NO evoked ON and OFF calcium transients in ASJ were completely abolished in daf-25(m362) mutants (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ability of ASJ neurons to detect NO requires DAF-11 and TAX-2/4 CNG channel localization to ciliated sensory endings.
source: Thus, the ability of ASJ neurons to detect NO requires DAF-11 and TAX-2/4 CNG channel localization to ciliated sensory endings.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that daf-25 mutants, which lack proper localization of these proteins, are defective in NO sensing.

claim: NO is sensed by ASJ as an external sensory cue.
source: Taken together, these results show that NO is sensed by ASJ as an external sensory cue.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that NO sensing requires functional ciliated sensory endings and proper localization of sensory proteins.

claim: NO covalently modifies reactive cysteine residues by S-nitrosylation (SNO).
source: NO covalently modifies reactive cysteine residues by S-nitrosylation (SNO).
evidence: This claim is based on established scientific knowledge about NO biochemistry.

claim: Protein-SNO modifications are reversed by two classes of enzymes, Thioredoxins (TRX) and nitrosoglutathione reductases (GSNOR).
source: Protein-SNO modifications are reversed by two classes of enzymes, Thioredoxins (TRX) and nitrosoglutathione reductases (GSNOR) (Benhar et al., 2009); consequently, protein-SNO adducts should accumulate in mutants lacking TRX and GSNOR.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Protein-SNO adducts should accumulate in mutants lacking TRX and GSNOR.
source: Protein-SNO modifications are reversed by two classes of enzymes, Thioredoxins (TRX) and nitrosoglutathione reductases (GSNOR) (Benhar et al., 2009); consequently, protein-SNO adducts should accumulate in mutants lacking TRX and GSNOR.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the known function of TRX and GSNOR in removing SNO modifications.

claim: trx-1 is exclusively expressed in the ASJ neurons.
source: We focused on the trx-1 gene (Figure 7A) because it is exclusively expressed in the ASJ neurons (Miranda-Vizuete et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The amplitude and duration of the NO-evoked ON transient in ASJ were both significantly increased in trx-1(jh127) null mutants.
source: The amplitude and duration of the NO-evoked ON transient in ASJ were both significantly increased in trx-1(jh127) null mutants (Figure 7A and B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and this defect was rescued by a single copy transgene restoring TRX-1 expression in ASJ neurons (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The defect in trx-1(jh127) null mutants was rescued by a single copy transgene restoring TRX-1 expression in ASJ neurons.
source: The amplitude and duration of the NO-evoked ON transient in ASJ were both significantly increased in trx-1(jh127) null mutants (Figure 7A and B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) and this defect was rescued by a single copy transgene restoring TRX-1 expression in ASJ neurons (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: In trx-1(nu517 C38S) mutants, the NO evoked OFF calcium transient was eliminated, whereas the ON transient was unaltered.
source: In trx-1(nu517 C38S) mutants, the NO evoked OFF calcium transient was eliminated, whereas the ON transient was unaltered (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: TRX-1's de-nitrosylating activity is required for ASJ to generate increased cytoplasmic calcium in response to removing NO.
source: These results suggest that TRX-1's de-nitrosylating activity is required for ASJ to generate increased cytoplasmic calcium in response to removing NO.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that a mutation in the de-nitrosylation active site eliminates the OFF response.

claim: The ASJ ON response of trx-1(jh127) null mutants was significantly larger than wild type.
source: Interestingly, the ASJ ON response of trx-1(jh127) null mutants was significantly larger than wild type whereas the ON response was unaltered in trx-1(nu517 C38S) mutants (compare Figure 7B and D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the null phenotype cannot be explained by decreased de-nitrosylation activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 7B, 7D, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The ON response was unaltered in trx-1(nu517 C38S) mutants.
source: Interestingly, the ASJ ON response of trx-1(jh127) null mutants was significantly larger than wild type whereas the ON response was unaltered in trx-1(nu517 C38S) mutants (compare Figure 7B and D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the null phenotype cannot be explained by decreased de-nitrosylation activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The null phenotype of trx-1 cannot be explained by decreased de-nitrosylation activity.
source: Interestingly, the ASJ ON response of trx-1(jh127) null mutants was significantly larger than wild type whereas the ON response was unaltered in trx-1(nu517 C38S) mutants (compare Figure 7B and D; Figure 7—figure supplement 1), suggesting that the null phenotype cannot be explained by decreased de-nitrosylation activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that the de-nitrosylation defective mutant has a different phenotype than the null mutant.

claim: TRX promotes nitrosylation of other proteins, and this trans-nitrosylation activity is eliminated by mutations altering Cys-72.
source: For example, TRX promotes nitrosylation of other proteins, and this trans-nitrosylation activity is eliminated by mutations altering Cys-72 (Mitchell and Marletta, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: A TRX-1(C72S) transgene failed to rescue the larger and more prolonged NO evoked ASJ ON response observed in trx-1 null mutants.
source: Unlike the wild type TRX-1 transgene, a TRX-1(C72S) transgene failed to rescue the larger and more prolonged NO evoked ASJ ON response observed in trx-1 null mutants (compare Figure 7C and E; Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figures 7C, 7E, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: The exaggerated amplitude and prolonged time course of the ASJ ON response to NO donor results from inactivation of TRX-1's trans-nitrosylation activity.
source: These results suggest that the exaggerated amplitude and prolonged time course of the ASJ ON response to NO donor results from inactivation of TRX-1's trans-nitrosylation activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that the C72S mutation fails to rescue the null phenotype.

claim: The OFF response was eliminated in both trx-1 mutants containing a mutation in the de-nitrosylation active site (nu517 C38S) and in gsnor-1 mutants.
source: The OFF response was eliminated in both trx-1 mutants containing a mutation in the de-nitrosylation active site (nu517 C38S) and in gsnor-1 mutants (which lack a second de-nitrosylating enzyme) (Benhar et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TRX-1 shapes ASJ's bi-phasic response to NO.
source: Collectively, our results suggest that TRX-1 shapes ASJ's bi-phasic response to NO (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that TRX-1 affects both ON and OFF responses.

claim: During NO exposure TRX-1's active site cysteines (C38/41) are oxidized, thereby decreasing de-nitrosylation.
source: Specifically, we propose that during NO exposure TRX-1's active site cysteines (C38/41) are oxidized, thereby decreasing de-nitrosylation (Engelman et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from prior literature about TRX oxidation.

claim: Oxidation of C38 and 41 promotes C72 nitrosylation.
source: Oxidation of C38 and 41 promotes C72 nitrosylation (Barglow et al., 2011), which increases trans-nitrosylation activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Oxidation of C38 and 41 increases trans-nitrosylation activity.
source: Oxidation of C38 and 41 promotes C72 nitrosylation (Barglow et al., 2011), which increases trans-nitrosylation activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the relationship between C72 nitrosylation and trans-nitrosylation activity.

claim: During NO exposure the net effect of TRX-1 would be increased trans-nitrosylation of protein substrates.
source: Thus, during NO exposure the net effect of TRX-1 would be increased trans-nitrosylation of protein substrates.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the proposed mechanism of TRX-1 oxidation and C72 nitrosylation.

claim: Trans-nitrosylated proteins inhibit the ON response.
source: We propose that these trans-nitrosylated proteins inhibit the ON response.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from experimental data.

claim: Following NO-removal, TRX-1 active site cysteines are reduced, thereby enhancing TRX-1's de-nitrosylation activity and inhibiting its trans-nitrosylation activity.
source: Following NO-removal, TRX-1 active site cysteines are reduced, thereby enhancing TRX-1's de-nitrosylation activity and inhibiting its trans-nitrosylation activity.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the proposed mechanism.

claim: Following NO removal, inhibitory SNO-protein adducts formed during NO exposure could be removed by TRX-1's de-nitrosylating activity, giving rise to the OFF response.
source: As a result, following NO removal, inhibitory SNO-protein adducts formed during NO exposure could be removed by TRX-1's de-nitrosylating activity, giving rise to the OFF response.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the proposed mechanism.

claim: The combined activities of TRX-1 produce ASJ's bi-phasic ON and OFF responses to NO.
source: Thus, the combined activities of TRX-1 produce ASJ's bi-phasic ON and OFF responses to NO.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data and the proposed mechanism.

claim: Mutations that diminish both the ON and OFF responses (i.e. daf-11, daf-25, and tax-4 mutations) were also deficient for both PA14 and NO avoidance.
source: Mutations that diminish both the ON and OFF responses (i.e. daf-11, daf-25, and tax-4 mutations) were also deficient for both PA14 and NO avoidance.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PA14 avoidance was decreased in gcy-27 mutants.
source: For example, PA14 avoidance was decreased in gcy-27 mutants, supporting the idea that OFF transients (which are deficient in gcy-27 mutants) are required to promote avoidance behavior.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: OFF transients are required to promote avoidance behavior.
source: For example, PA14 avoidance was decreased in gcy-27 mutants, supporting the idea that OFF transients (which are deficient in gcy-27 mutants) are required to promote avoidance behavior.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that gcy-27 mutants, which lack OFF transients, have decreased PA14 avoidance.

claim: PA14 avoidance was unaffected in the de-nitrosylation defective mutants, trx-1(nu517 C38S) and gsnor-1, which also lack the OFF response.
source: On the other hand, PA14 avoidance was unaffected in the de-nitrosylation defective mutants, trx-1(nu517 C38S) and gsnor-1, which also lack the OFF response.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: PA14 avoidance was significantly reduced in mutants deficient for trans-nitrosylation, trx-1(C72S) and trx-1(jh127) null mutants, which have a heightened and prolonged ON response.
source: Finally, PA14 avoidance was significantly reduced in mutants deficient for trans-nitrosylation, trx-1(C72S) and trx-1(jh127) null mutants, which have a heightened and prolonged ON response.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The temporal structure of ASJ's NO response plays an important role in PA14 avoidance.
source: Collectively, these results support the idea that the temporal structure of ASJ's NO response plays an important role in PA14 avoidance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that different mutations affecting the temporal structure of NO responses have different effects on PA14 avoidance.

claim: Bacterially produced CO2 was utilized as a contextual cue to promote C. elegans avoidance of another pathogen, Serratia marascens.
source: A prior study suggested that bacterially produced CO2 was utilized as a contextual cue to promote C. elegans avoidance of another pathogen, Serratia marascens (Brandt and Ringstad, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Environmental CO2 indicates proximity to metabolically active bacteria.
source: These authors proposed that environmental CO2 indicates proximity to metabolically active bacteria, and that pathogen avoidance is mediated by the coincident detection of CO2 in conjunction with other virulence factors.
evidence: This claim is based on a proposal from prior literature.

claim: Pathogen avoidance is mediated by the coincident detection of CO2 in conjunction with other virulence factors.
source: These authors proposed that environmental CO2 indicates proximity to metabolically active bacteria, and that pathogen avoidance is mediated by the coincident detection of CO2 in conjunction with other virulence factors.
evidence: This claim is based on a proposal from prior literature.

claim: A coincidence detection strategy would allow worms to actively feed on avirulent bacteria while avoiding ingestion of pathogenic bacteria.
source: Such a coincidence detection strategy is proposed to optimize the ability of C. elegans to forage for nutritional resources since it would allow worms to actively feed on avirulent bacteria while avoiding ingestion of pathogenic bacteria.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from the proposed coincidence detection mechanism.

claim: C. elegans avoidance of PA14 is mediated by a coincidence detection strategy.
source: Our results suggest that C. elegans avoidance of PA14 is mediated by a similar coincidence detection strategy.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from experimental data.

claim: Recent exposure to NO enhances the repulsive effects of other PA14 metabolites, for example, phenazine compounds.
source: In particular, we propose that recent exposure to NO enhances the repulsive effects of other PA14 metabolites, for example, phenazine compounds (Meisel and Kim, 2014).
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from experimental data.

claim: C. elegans discriminates between benign and pathogenic microbes by coincident detection of multiple bacterial metabolites, including both CO2 and NO.
source: Thus, our results combined with this prior study suggest that C. elegans discriminates between benign and pathogenic microbes by coincident detection of multiple bacterial metabolites, including both CO2 and NO.
evidence: This claim is speculative and based on inference from experimental data and prior literature.

claim: The NO evoked ASJ OFF response was significantly diminished in the gsnor-1 mutants, whereas the ON response remained.
source: The NO evoked ASJ OFF response was significantly diminished in the gsnor-1 mutants, whereas the ON response remained (Figure 7F, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Analysis of trx-1 and gsnor-1 mutants both suggest that protein de-nitrosylation is required for the ASJ response evoked by removing NO.
source: Thus, analysis of trx-1 and gsnor-1 mutants both suggest that protein de-nitrosylation is required for the ASJ response evoked by removing NO.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that mutations in both de-nitrosylating enzymes eliminate the OFF response.

claim: PA14 avoidance was significantly reduced in trx-1(jh127) null mutants.
source: PA14 avoidance was significantly reduced in trx-1(jh127) null mutants (Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The PA14 avoidance defect in trx-1(jh127) null mutants was rescued by a single copy transgene expressing wild type TRX-1.
source: This PA14 avoidance defect was rescued by a single copy transgene expressing wild type TRX-1 but was not rescued by the TRX-1(C72S) transgene (Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The PA14 avoidance defect in trx-1(jh127) null mutants was not rescued by the TRX-1(C72S) transgene.
source: This PA14 avoidance defect was rescued by a single copy transgene expressing wild type TRX-1 but was not rescued by the TRX-1(C72S) transgene (Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: PA14 avoidance was unaltered in the two de-nitrosylation defective mutants, trx-1(nu517 C38S) and gsnor-1(nu518).
source: By contrast, PA14 avoidance was unaltered in the two de-nitrosylation defective mutants, trx-1(nu517 C38S) and gsnor-1(nu518) (Figure 7G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: TRX-1's trans-nitrosylation activity is required for PA14 avoidance.
source: These results suggest that TRX-1's trans-nitrosylation activity is required for PA14 avoidance.
evidence: This claim is inferred from experimental data showing that mutations affecting trans-nitrosylation activity affect PA14 avoidance.
